raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male with Crohn's disease on azathioprine 100 mg daily in longstanding clinical remission presented to an outpatient gastroenterologist for sudden onset of right upper quadrant abdominal pain 8/10 in severity with radiation to his back. He also endorsed fevers but denied nausea, vomiting, any change in bowel movements, or rectal bleeding. Five months prior to admission, the patient had traveled to northern India and, while there, contracted "traveler's diarrhea," which was self-limited and treated with loperamide.
At a gastroenterology clinic, a right upper quadrant ultrasound revealed a 46 mm hypoechoic lesion in the liver, correlating with the area of the patient's pain. The patient was then referred to the emergency room for further evaluation.
In the emergency room, the patient was afebrile without hypotension or tachycardia. Labs revealed a white blood cell count of 9.91 x 103/muL, hemoglobin of 13.4 g/dL, platelets of 277 x 103/muL, aspartate aminotransferase of 18 U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 22 U/L, total bilirubin of 0.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 64 U/L, and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 23.2 mg/dL. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen/pelvis showed a 6.0 cm x 5.0 cm low/intermediate density lesion in segment 4A/B of the liver with a thick marginal rim and adjacent parenchymal inflammation and biliary prominence (Figure 1). Due to concern for pyogenic abscess, the patient underwent drainage of the abscess by interventional radiology with 110 cc of reported "pus" removed "without anchovy appearance." A drainage catheter was placed.
Following drainage, the patient was started on empiric ertapenem 1 g IV daily and metronidazole 500 mg PO TID. Azathioprine was held. Bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures were negative from the drained fluid. Blood cultures were also negative, except one drawn 2 days into admission that resulted positive for Staphylococcus epidermidis, presumed to be a contaminant. Stool exam for ova and parasites resulted four days after admission with protozoa, later identified as Entamoeba coli trophozoites. The patient's second stool sample was positive for nonpathogenic protozoa, and the third stool sample was negative.
The patient was discharged on ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO BID and metronidazole 500 mg PO TID for an anticipated three-week antibiotic course from the day of drainage. Entamoeba histolytica IgG antibody returned positive three days after discharge, supporting the diagnosis of amebic liver abscess. The Entamoeba histolytica stool antigen returned negative. Echinococcus and Strongyloides serologies also returned negative. The drain was removed by interventional radiology 1 week after discharge. Repeat CT scan of the abdomen/pelvis 2 weeks after discharge revealed near complete resolution of the abscess with no drainable fluid collection (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male with Crohn's disease in remission on azathioprine presented with sudden-onset severe (8/10) right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to his back and fevers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to his outpatient gastroenterologist with acute 8/10 right upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back accompanied by fevers, without gastrointestinal symptoms. After an outpatient right upper quadrant ultrasound identified a 46-mm hypoechoic liver lesion correlating with the site of pain, he was referred to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Crohn's disease in longstanding clinical remission maintained on oral azathioprine 100 mg daily. Travel history to northern India 5 months prior to admission, where he experienced self-limited traveler's diarrhea treated with loperamide.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sudden severe right upper quadrant pain (8/10) radiating to the back and fevers. Negative for nausea, vomiting, change in bowel habits, or rectal bleeding. Home medication: azathioprine 100 mg daily.

objective.physical_examination: In the emergency department, the patient was afebrile, normotensive, and non-tachycardic.
objective.routine_investigations: Outpatient right upper quadrant ultrasound showed a 46-mm hypoechoic hepatic lesion. Emergency room labs: WBC 9.91 x 10^3/uL, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 277 x 10^3/uL, AST 18 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 64 U/L, and elevated CRP 23.2 mg/dL. Blood cultures were negative (one bottle at day 2 grew contaminant Staphylococcus epidermidis). Three serial stool ova and parasite exams showed nonpathogenic Entamoeba coli trophozoites in two samples and negative third sample; stool E. histolytica antigen was negative; Echinococcus and Strongyloides serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 6.0 cm x 5.0 cm low/intermediate-density lesion in hepatic segment 4A/B with a thick marginal rim, adjacent parenchymal inflammation, and biliary prominence. Interventional Radiology performed percutaneous catheter drainage, evacuating 110 cc of purulent fluid ('without anchovy appearance'); bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures of the aspirate were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Serum Entamoeba histolytica IgG antibody returned positive 3 days post-discharge (with bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, Echinococcus, and Strongyloides infections ruled out), confirming an amoebic liver abscess in an immunosuppressed Crohn's disease patient 5 months after travel to India. Azathioprine was held, 110 cc of pus was drained via IR catheter, and initial inpatient ertapenem (1 g IV daily) plus oral metronidazole (500 mg PO TID) was transitioned upon discharge to a 3-week course of oral ciprofloxacin (750 mg BID) and metronidazole (500 mg TID). The hepatic drain was removed 1 week after discharge, and repeat abdominal CT at 2 weeks demonstrated near-complete resolution of the abscess.
